title: It is Time to Create the New
author: Kathleen Schafer
summary: Schafer declares that a beloved oak has come down, and in the rubble of that loss, she recognizes a moment of unquestionable clarity: the old way is not coming back. For decades, many have survived in systems that demanded speed over wisdom, performance over presence, power over care. Success within misalignment doesn't make the system whole; it only means becoming skillful at surviving what was never designed for flourishing. Schafer argues the question shifts from how to renovate what has outlived its usefulness to what wants to emerge instead. She rejects the old paradigm of individual leaders commanding followers toward promised futures and proposes distributed citizen leadership: ordinary people taking responsibility for the life they're shaping together, rooted in alignment and integrity rather than performance. This shift requires releasing deeply embedded stories about who has the right to lead, where change originates, and what participation looks like. She commits to the work of creating containers where people can return to themselves and then return differently to the world, guided by truth, care, and a willingness to take the next steps toward a more human future.
points: Old paradigms (performance over presence, certainty over wisdom, power over care) can be survived but not transcended; the new emerges not from renovation but from fundamental reorientation.

Citizen leadership distributes authority from charismatic figures to ordinary people willing to take responsibility for the places they inhabit; it is built from alignment and integrity, not performance.
The shift from waiting for institutional permission to building what aligns with truth requires releasing old stories about who belongs in leadership.
Creating the new requires stopping long enough to hear what the heart knows before it has been validated, and then taking grounded action rooted in that knowing.
Leadership in this moment moves from dominance, certainty, and charisma toward contribution, integrity, and care.
quotes: There is something about standing in the rubble of what you loved, something that was strong, that sheltered real things, that meant something, that burns away every last reason to keep waiting. There comes a moment when we know, without needing any more evidence, that the old way is not coming back.

For a long time, many of us have lived inside systems that asked us to contort ourselves in order to belong. Systems that rewarded speed over wisdom, performance over presence, certainty over truth, and power over care. But succeeding inside something misaligned does not make it whole.

I am no longer interested in leadership that asks people to follow a single person toward a promised future. That too belongs to an older paradigm. What I am interested in is helping set the conditions for the steps we need to take together. Not to be followed. Not to be admired from afar.

This is not a small shift. It requires us to release some very old stories. The story that leadership belongs to the loudest person in the room. The story that real change only comes from institutions. The story that our role is to watch, critique, and wait.

I believe we are being asked to become citizen leaders in the fullest sense of that phrase. Not political actors in the narrow sense, but human beings willing to take responsibility for the life we are shaping together.

While none of us can create the whole of the new alone, each of us is responsible for the part we are here to bring.” Archived from Kathleen Schafer Substack (Extraordinarily Ordinary) on May 3, 2026 by Tim.
